Maren read it in the lantern room with the great lens still turning beside her, then polished the brass out of habit, though no hand would need to trim a wick again.

She still climbed the stair at dusk. There was nothing to light, but her eyes knew the moment the sea went from pewter to ink better than they knew a darkened room, and the tide did not seem to have heard that the keeper had been retired. She would stand on the gallery as the wind came round from the west, and the fishing boats would go out past the skerries with their lamps lit, and she would count them by the way her mother had taught her to count the seconds between flashes.

The skippers said the new lamp never failed and never wandered from its rhythm. She believed them. She still watched the boats come home in the grey of morning, naming each by the set of its wheelhouse, and once young Fallon raised a hand from the deck of the Marigold, which was either habit or kindness, and Maren did not go inside.

What surprised her was how the boats kept finding the harbour without anyone to keep the light for them. She had thought herself the beam. Now she understood she had mostly been the one who watched it fall on the water. The coast had never needed her hand on the winding gear; it had needed someone on the gallery to believe each night that the watching mattered.
